Egyptian deities fascinate me. I definitely find the way the Egyptians perceived the gods as among the top curiosities I have for them. I bring this up because I believe your title to be wrong. Whereas the Greeks and Romans perceived their gods as superhuman beings that wield certain universal realities, such as the seas, or time, the Egyptian gods were the other way around. They were the universal truths made manifest, which is why they had several ways to depict the gods, and the gods had hybridized forms. A cow held the symbolic meaning of fertility, so a cow represented the goddess of fertility, who was also represented as humanoid with a cow's head, because she is the human concept of fertility.

It's really a minor quibble, and I'm definitely not trying to make you feel bad or anything of the like. If anything I applaud a scholar in the subject. I'm just trying to open you up to considering new facts. The ancient Egyptian faith was complex, and intermingled modern concepts of divinity with ancient, I would argue prehistoric, ideas of spirituality and the interlinking of the natural, human, and divine. It's fascinating and I encourage you to continue to learn!

"the Egyptian gods were the other way around. They were the universal truths made manifest, which is why they had several ways to depict the gods, and the gods had hybridized forms. A cow held the symbolic meaning of fertility, so a cow represented the goddess of fertility, who was also represented as humanoid with a cow's head, because she is the human concept of fertility." Can you expound?

There really isn't much to expound on beyond that. It was believed that the gods themselves took on any form necessary to achieve a desired end. There was no definitive form that the gods would always take, because, to put it simply, to manifest themselves to a full degree in our realm would shatter it. That would be taking all of the justice in the world and concentrating it in one single entity, or all of the love in the world, or all of the sky, or the flooding of the Nile. Instead the Egyptian gods would manifest themselves only partly, as a gust of wind, or a small river. Something that carries the meaning of their existence in that moment. There is a story about a man whose wife tried to cheat on him with his brother, and then would go to blame that brother for instigating the affair. When the brother was being chased off, he made an appeal to the all seeing eye of Horus, who knows all that is truth, and Horus took pity on the man, and manifested a river with crocodiles in it, between the brothers, so that they could safely talk it out without the threat of violence between them.

That's what I mean when I say that the gods are simply the universal truths. They act to enable and ensure that those truths are distributed across the world. They do not wield these powers as entities separate from them, as Zeus or Aphrodite might. In a short summary: The Egyptians believed that there are three worlds: the world of the natural, the world of the human, and the world of the divine, and all three of these worlds are distinct but necessarily linked. Without the natural world, no physical existence could be, without the human world, no divinity could be as the divines are fed and fueled by human belief, and without the divinities, so much could not exist to ensure that proper balance was made in the world. The divine world, are where realities such as life and death, intelligent thought, and even the concept of existence itself, spawn from, and those ideas have names. The concept of justice is Ma'at, and Ma'at is also a goddess, for example. This is why in Egyptian mythos, you generally see the gods are more or less without personality. They only interact when it means initiating a necessary reality in the human world.
